source.title_on_document: Revolution or inflated expectations? Exploring the impact of generative AI on ideation in a practical sustainability context

supplement.where: Appendix printed at the end of the article, pp. 11-13 (Tables A1-A3, Figs. A1-A2, and the prompts). The paper refers to no separate online supplement.
supplement.holds: Table A1 (number of ideas, mean and SD of novelty, value, feasibility, and investability per condition, and Kruskal-Wallis statistics with p-values), Table A2 (correlations among the four dimensions), Table A3 (number of topics and the three most frequent topics per condition), Fig. A1 (boxplots, which also show a sixth condition labeled Experts-AI), Fig. A2 (word cloud of topics), and the prompts. The chi-square p-values and the top-idea counts (Figs. 2 and 3) are in the main text. The paper reports no standard errors and no pairwise tests.

paper_design_summary: In a project with BSH Home Appliances, the authors evaluated 146 sustainable-packaging ideas from five described conditions: three ChatGPT-4 conditions run by the researchers (30 ideas each), ten BSH experts without AI input (30 ideas), and the same ten experts supplied with AI-generated ideas (26 ideas). Five other BSH experts rated the outputs on 5-point scales for novelty, value, feasibility, and investability, and the authors coded topics (pp. 4-5, Section 3.2; p. 7, Section 4.2; pp. 11-12, Tables A1 and A3). No random assignment or randomized condition order is reported; the workshop groups were formed by department, the subdomains were swapped between conditions, and the second group's condition order is ambiguous (p. 5, Section 3.2).

studies.label: ChatGPT-4-only ideas (AI, AI-AI, WoS-AI) versus expert-workshop ideas without AI (Experts)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people. The researchers generated the AI, AI-AI, and WoS-AI ideas with ChatGPT-4 and fixed prompts, and ten BSH experts produced the Experts ideas in a workshop without AI. The comparison is between sources of ideas.
assignment.quote: To do this, we generated ideas using pre-tested prompts directly with ChatGPT and by organizing a 2-h ideation session with ten BSH experts from different departments concerned with sustainable packaging.

arms.name: AI
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 interface with a context-specific prompt (role, context, task, boundaries; about 250 words per idea); 30 ideas, 15 per subdomain.

arms.name: AI-AI
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 refines the AI-condition ideas with SCAMPER-inspired instructions (Section 3.2 names substitution, combination, and removal of features; the printed prompts are headed Substitute, Combine, and Add), 5 ideas per instruction; 30 ideas.

arms.name: WoS-AI
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 prompt seeded with themes from 979 Web of Science articles (92 themes per Section 3.2; the printed prompt says 83 topics); 30 ideas.

arms.name: Experts
arms.description: Ten BSH sustainable-packaging experts in two groups, each group on one subdomain; nominal technique (about 15 min writing alone, 15 min sharing, 15 min refining); no AI; 30 ideas.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The only human ideators are the ten workshop experts; the three AI arms have no participants. The analysis unit is the idea (30 per arm). Five separate BSH experts rated all 146 ideas.
participants.who: Ten sustainable-packaging experts from six BSH departments (development, logistics, procurement, production, quality, design), eight male and two female, based at five German BSH sites, all very experienced in sustainable packaging. The raters were five other BSH experts with a more managerial view who had not attended the workshop.
participants.quote: Ten sustainable packaging experts from six BSH departments (development, logistics, procurement, production, quality, and design) joined the workshop.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 through the ChatGPT interface (footnote 3: OpenAI API outputs at temperatures 0.7, 0.8, and 0.9 showed no substantial differences)
ai_tool.how_used: The researchers prompted ChatGPT-4 to generate the AI-arm outputs; no study participant received AI assistance in these S1 arms (pp. 4-5, Section 3.2).

task.description: Ideas for sustainable transport packaging of home appliances in two subdomains: material-based solutions (EPS-free, plastic-free, material reduction) and systemic solutions (reuse and recycling systems). Each AI condition has 15 ideas per subdomain.
task.duration: Experts: about 15 min individual writing, 15 min sharing, and 15 min refining within a 2-h workshop. AI conditions: not applicable.

studies.label: Same ten experts supplied with AI-generated ideas (AI-Experts) versus their unassisted condition (Experts)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No random assignment to AI or randomized condition order is reported. The ten experts were split into two groups, allocating employees from the same departments to different groups. Both groups completed Experts and AI-Experts on different subdomains. The first group worked without AI on material-based solutions and, after a long break, with AI ideas on systemic solutions. The subdomains were swapped between groups, but 'the other way round' does not explicitly establish the second group's condition order (p. 5, Section 3.2).
assignment.quote: For example, the first group generated ideas in the material-based solutions subdomain described in the Experts condition, and then, after a long break, in the systemic solutions subdomain described in the AI–Experts condition.

arms.name: AI-Experts
arms.description: The ten workshop experts, in their two groups, received the AI-condition ideas as inspiration and generated 26 ideas; the material-based and systemic subdomains were swapped relative to the Experts condition (p. 5, Section 3.2).

arms.name: Experts
arms.description: The same ten experts without AI input, nominal technique (about 15 min alone, 15 min sharing, 15 min refining); 30 ideas.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The same ten experts took part in both conditions, in two groups whose sizes are not stated. The analysis is at the idea level (30 Experts and 26 AI-Experts ideas).
participants.who: Ten BSH sustainable-packaging experts (eight male, two female) from six departments, based at BSH sites in Germany.
participants.quote: We separated the participants into two groups, allocating employees from the same departments to different groups.

ai_tool.how_used: Participants received the AI-generated ideas from the first (AI) condition as inspiration before generating their own ideas; they did not interact with the model.

task.description: Sustainable transport-packaging ideas for home appliances; each group worked on one subdomain in the Experts condition and on the other in the AI-Experts condition (p. 5, Section 3.2).
task.duration: Within a 2-h workshop (p. 4, Section 3.2). The Experts condition used about 15 min individual writing, 15 min sharing, and 15 min refinement. The first group's AI-Experts round followed a long break; the AI-Experts duration and the second group's condition order are not stated explicitly (p. 5, Section 3.2).

eligibility.reason: S1 compares researcher-generated ChatGPT-4 outputs with expert-workshop outputs, rather than assigning people to AI assistance (pp. 4-5, Section 3.2). S2 compares the same ten experts with and without supplied AI ideas; groups were formed by department and no random assignment or randomized condition order is reported (p. 5, Section 3.2). Thus criterion 1 is not met on the available report. Ten unique human ideators were analyzed, not 146 people: 146 is the reported number of ideas, and the five separate evaluators do not count toward the participant threshold (p. 5, Section 3.2; p. 11, Table A1). Criterion 2 is not met regardless of the unresolved condition-order detail. Criterion 3 is met because experts scored the generated ideas for novelty and other output qualities on 5-point scales (p. 5, Section 3.2). The main context class is ai_vs_human; S2 is quasi_people/observational context.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT-4 ideas were rated more novel than ideas from a ten-expert BSH workshop (mean novelty AI 3.13, AI-AI 3.21, WoS-AI 3.08 vs Experts 2.73; Kruskal-Wallis across five conditions p = 0.009) but less feasible (2.39 to 2.43 vs 2.81; p = 0.076), and the same experts given AI ideas as inspiration scored lower on value (2.72 vs 3.19) and feasibility (2.35 vs 2.81) and had the fewest top novel-and-valuable ideas (2 of 26 vs 11 of 30) (p. 11, Table A1; p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 7, Fig. 3).
open_questions: Text and Fig. 2 disagree on three top-idea counts: the text gives 22 of 30 AI ideas as top on novelty, 26 of 30 Experts ideas as top on value, and twelve Experts ideas as top on investability, while Fig. 2 plots 20, 23, and 14 (p. 6). Which is correct?

Fig. A1 (p. 11) plots a sixth condition, Experts-AI, absent from the five conditions in Section 3.2, Fig. 1, and Table A1. The prompt heading on p. 12 also reads 'AI-AI und Experts-AI' and refers to ideas previously generated by employees. Which observations and conditions entered each omnibus test, and how should this extra condition be interpreted? No numerical expected counts are printed in Fig. 2; they should not be reconstructed as reported statistics.

The second expert group did the procedure 'the other way round' (p. 5, Section 3.2). The phrase 'the previous round of expert-based idea generation' suggests unassisted ideation first, but the second group's condition order is not explicit. Authors would need to confirm both groups' orders and whether any condition-order assignment was randomized; counterbalancing alone would not satisfy criterion 1.
How the five raters' scores were combined per idea, whether the raters knew each idea's condition, and inter-rater agreement are not stated.

Section 3.2 says 92 themes were condensed from the Web of Science articles, while the WoS-AI prompt (p. 13) lists 83 topics. Section 3.2 says the AI-AI instructions asked for substitution, combination, and removal of features, while the printed prompts (pp. 12-13) are headed Substitute, Combine, and Add.
notes: One dataset is described as containing 146 ideas (AI 30, AI-AI 30, AI-Experts 26, Experts 30, WoS-AI 30; p. 5, Section 3.2; p. 11, Table A1). Its two design components are retained as S1 (ai_vs_human) and S2 (quasi_people); they share the Experts arm and the same ten people and must not be counted as independent samples. Table A1 reports Kruskal-Wallis statistics alongside five condition rows, and Section 4.1 describes five-group chi-square comparisons; because Fig. A1 additionally plots Experts-AI, the exact condition membership used in the tests is not verified. No pairwise tests or participant-level statistics are reported. Figs. 2 and 3 were inspected directly in the PDF: the recorded figure counts describe plotted dots, not printed numeric labels, and the conflicts with the p. 6 prose are retained. Approximate expected-count calculations were removed from open_questions because they are not reported statistics. For the set-level topic outcomes, n_units is null; the number of ideas in each pool remains in diversity_detail.computed_over (pp. 11-12, Tables A1 and A3). For the expert evaluation, environmental- and financial-impact sections of AI outputs were removed (p. 12, note above the prompts). The approximately 20-min focus group and the next-day email survey concern perceptions, not output scores; Fig. 1 reports a 100 percent survey response rate (pp. 4-5). Table A2 reports a novelty-feasibility correlation of -0.41 (p. 11). No exclusions are reported. Final review covered the full markdown and appendices and checked the relevant PDF pages and figures. No c055 challenge files were present; the final challenge-resolution array and its counters are therefore empty/zero. All 11 reconciliation differences have status resolved, and the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged. The five open questions are assessed individually in final.open_items. Their possible relevance to an individual criterion is distinguished from the definitive core exclusion for fewer than 50 people.

open_items.item: Top-idea counts conflict between the prose and Fig. 2: AI novelty 22 versus a plotted 20, Experts value 26 versus 23, and Experts investability twelve versus 14 (p. 6, Section 4.1 and Fig. 2). Author confirmation of the underlying counts is needed. This concerns reported results; it changes none of the three eligibility criteria.

Fig. A1 contains Experts-AI in addition to the five conditions described in Section 3.2 and Table A1; the p. 12 prompt heading also names Experts-AI (pp. 5, 11-12). Authors must identify the extra condition and the observations and conditions used for each omnibus test. The discrepancy does not itself establish additional human participants or randomized AI assistance and does not affect the stated eligibility criteria.

The second group's condition order is ambiguous in 'the other way round' (p. 5, Section 3.2). Authors would need to document both groups' orders and any randomization of condition order. This bears on criterion 1: fixed or merely counterbalanced order does not qualify, and randomized order is not reported. Criterion 2 still fails with ten unique ideators, so the core exclusion is definitive.

Aggregation of the five raters' scores, blinding to idea source, and inter-rater agreement are not stated (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2; p. 11, Table A1). Authors must supply the rating protocol and reliability information. These affect interpretation and precision, but criterion 3 is already met because actual ideas were scored for novelty and other output qualities.

The methods report 92 Web of Science themes and AI-AI substitution/combination/removal, whereas the printed prompts use 83 topics and Substitute/Combine/Add (p. 5, Section 3.2; pp. 12-13, Prompts). Authors must identify the prompts and topic list actually used. These implementation discrepancies do not affect random assignment, the human participant count, or whether outputs were scored.
